---
title: "How to read this documentation"
---

This is the model documentation for the SME Lending Decision Platform: one small-business
lending book of {{< var score.n_applicants >}} synthetic applicants, one scorecard, and four
decision modules that consume it. It is written for a model validator. It is also written so
that a learner can see what a validator expects, and why.

## The order: SR 11-7

The chapters follow the order of the US supervisory guidance on model risk management,
SR 11-7 (OCC 2011-12): what the models are and how much they matter, what they are for, the
data, how they depend on each other, one chapter per model, then implementation, the use of
AI agents, and sign-off. The [crosswalk](../reference/crosswalk.qmd) maps each section to
OSFI E-23 (Canada) and PRA SS1/23 (UK).

## The template

Every model chapter (D4 to D8) has the same nine parts, so a validator can find the same
thing in the same place in every chapter:

1. **Purpose and use** — the decision supported, the users, the population, prohibited uses.
2. **Data and sample** — sources, split, populations, leakage controls, exclusions.
3. **Methodology and alternatives** — the method, what else was considered and why not.
4. **Assumptions** — each one, its evidence, and what breaks if it fails.
5. **Performance** — discrimination with an interval, rank-ordering, calibration,
   stability, a benchmark and the ceiling, each with the population it was measured on.
6. **Sensitivity and stress** — refits with fewer inputs; what a gate failure means.
7. **Limitations and compensating controls** — numbered findings, each with an owner.
8. **Monitoring plan** — metrics, thresholds, frequency and the action on a breach.
9. **Gate record** — the committed gate, where it is asserted, where it is recomputed.

The template lives in `wiki/mdd/_template/`: nine short files, each holding the brief for
its part. To start a new chapter, copy the folder and replace each brief with prose.

## Where the numbers come from

No number in these pages is typed by hand. Each one is a fact computed through the
platform's own module functions and stored, with the population it was measured on, in
`wiki/facts/facts.json`. The pages print facts by name, and the
[fact index](../reference/facts.qmd) lists every one with its source and population.

`python verify.py` recomputes the facts from the committed models and data every time it
runs, and fails naming the key if any page would print a stale value. A lint fails the
build on any hand-typed metric. Two consequences for a reader:

- if a number here disagrees with the code, that is a defect, and `verify.py` should
  already have caught it;
- an AUC is never printed without the population it was measured on, because the same
  model scores very differently on applicants and on the loans the bank actually books.
